paraphrase: Fourth upadeśa (114 segments): homage and the announcement of the order of samādhi (4.1-2); synonyms and definitions of samādhi and rājayoga (4.3-7); the role of the guru, of śakti and of the middle channel (4.8-20); the mutual dependence of mind and breath and laya as the lord of the breath (4.21-34); śāmbhavī and khecarī as states (4.35-49, largely summary-only); contemplations that dissolve the mind (4.50-62); closing of the survey of methods (4.63-64); nāda-attention: its method, its four stages of ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya and niṣpatti, the inner sounds, the images of the mind as an animal (4.65-99); the soundless as the highest (4.100-102); haṭha, laya and rājayoga related and the marks of the yogin in samādhi (4.103-113); and the closing warning against empty talk of knowledge (4.114).

paraphrase: The Haṭhapradīpikā presents its whole body of practice (posture, purification, breath practices, mudrās and attention to the inner sound) as haṭha, taught 'solely for the sake of rājayoga' (1.2), that is, for the state of samādhi in which mind and breath dissolve and the self and the mind become one (4.3-7); haṭha and rājayoga are said to depend on each other (2.76), and those who practise haṭha without knowing rājayoga are said to labour without fruit (4.79). Marks of purport (ṣaḍ-liṅga): (1) Opening and closing: the teaching opens by stating that haṭha is for rājayoga (1.2) and closes by saying that all haṭha and laya means are for its accomplishment (4.103) and by the seed-field-water image (4.104), with a last warning against empty talk of knowledge (4.114). (2) Repetition: the same relation of haṭha to rājayoga is stated at 1.2, 1.67, 2.76, 3.126, 4.79 and 4.103; the necessity of the guru and of secrecy recurs (1.11, 1.14, 2.23, 3.9, 3.78-79, 3.129, 4.8-9). (3) Novelty: the text ranks its chief items (1.43) and puts attention to the inner sound as the chief of ways of laya (4.66); it gives the teaching of the mutual dependence of mind and breath (4.21-25). (4) Stated result: rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, the natural state (4.3-4), the yogin's marks in samādhi (4.106-113), and 'let there be liberation or not, here is unbroken happiness' (4.78). (5) Praise (arthavāda), to be read as rhetorical, not as doctrine: the great adepts who have broken the staff of Death (1.9), claims for postures (1.31, 1.47), for the mudrās (3.8, 3.16, 3.29-30), for khecarī (3.38-40), and the samādhi-yogin who cannot be slain by weapons (4.113). (6) Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): the argument from the joint movement of mind and breath (2.2, 4.21-25, 4.28-29) and the similes of salt in water and camphor in fire (4.5, 4.59).
